step1_summary: Symptom details: • Began yesterday mid-morning (≈24 h duration so far) • Unilateral – left posterior/occipital region • Quality: throbbing, ‘intense’ • Severity: 8/10 • Gradual build-up, then persistent; no clear diurnal or positional variation • No associated nausea, vomiting, visual changes, photophobia, phonophobia, focal weakness, numbness, speech difficulty, fever, chills, neck stiffness, rash • Ibuprofen (Nurofen) provided little relief • Normal appetite, hydration and sleep; able to work but with difficulty
Medications/allergies: no regular drugs; took single dose of ibuprofen; no known allergies
Family history: mother has hypertension and migraines
Social history: 28-year-old female designer; lives with partner; does not smoke, drink alcohol or use recreational drugs
Vital signs / exam: none recorded (remote visit); no objective neurological or meningeal findings elicited
Labs / imaging: none obtained or mentioned

V: Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH): sudden new unilateral severe headache could represent sentinel bleed, though description less abrupt than classic ‘thunderclap’.
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis: new persistent headache in young woman, unilateral; risk factors unknown (e.g. OCP) but worth considering.
I: Viral or bacterial meningitis: acute headache can be presenting sign; absence of fever/neck stiffness makes less likely.
Acute sinusitis (ethmoid/sphenoid): can cause unilateral occipital headaches but usually with nasal symptoms.
N: Intracranial mass lesion (primary or metastatic brain tumour): new unexplained headache in adult warrants exclusion, especially if progressive or refractory to analgesia.
D: Tension-type headache: common, can be throbbing but usually bilateral; stress or muscle tension could fit.
Cervicogenic (musculoskeletal/degenerative neck origin) headache: pain often occipital and unilateral.
I2: Medication-over-use headache: unlikely – minimal analgesic exposure.
Caffeine withdrawal: if recent change in intake.
C: Chiari I malformation: can present in young adults with occipital headaches worsened by Valsalva.
A: Migraine without aura: classic unilateral throbbing headache; family history present.
E: Hypertensive headache: family history but patient’s BP unknown.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Unilateral throbbing moderate-to-severe headache with functional impairment and positive family history, in a young woman with no focal deficits, fits common migraine presentation despite absence of nausea/photophobia in this episode.
supporting_evidence: Family history of migraines in mother
Age and sex typical for migraine onset
No systemic or focal neurological signs to suggest secondary cause
opposing_evidence: No nausea, photophobia, phonophobia or visual aura reported
Minimal response to NSAID (although single dose may be inadequate)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Common primary headache; can be precipitated by stress or posture and may be refractory to single NSAID dose. Lack of autonomic or focal features supports this possibility.
opposing_evidence: Pain is unilateral and described as throbbing (tension headaches are classically bilateral, ‘band-like’ and non-pulsatile)
Severity 8/10 higher than typical tension headache

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Unilateral occipital pain can originate from upper cervical structures; common in people with desk jobs (designer) and poor posture.
supporting_evidence: Sedentary occupation that may strain neck muscles
opposing_evidence: No neck pain or restricted movement noted

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Any new progressive headache warrants exclusion of space-occupying lesion, but very acute onset (<24 h) and lack of neurological deficits make this less likely.
supporting_evidence: New onset headache in adult with no prior history
opposing_evidence: Only 1-day history – tumours usually produce subacute/chronic headaches
No morning worsening, vomiting, or focal deficits

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Dangerous vascular cause of sudden severe headache; must be kept in mind though presentation lacks classic sudden ‘worst ever’ or neck stiffness.
supporting_evidence: First such headache in life (sentinel bleed possible)
opposing_evidence: Pain built up gradually rather than instant ‘thunderclap’
No neck stiffness, photophobia, vomiting or syncope
